steps.title: Code to Hardware
steps.markdownContent:
Now let's connect words in code to physical hardware pins!

Here is one of the most famous instructions in all of robotics:

```cpp
digitalWrite(13, HIGH);
```

Let's break down what each word tells the Arduino:
- `digitalWrite`: The action command! Tells the Arduino to send power to a digital pin.
- `(` and `)`: Parentheses that hold the details.
- `13`: The target pin! Digital Pin 13 is connected to the built-in amber LED on your board.
- `,`: A comma that separates the pin number from the state.
- `HIGH`: Turn power ON (+5 Volts)! (If we wrote `LOW`, it would turn power OFF).
- `;`: The semicolon! Every statement ends with a semicolon, just like a period ends a sentence.

Let's see how typing letters on a keyboard actually pushes real electricity out of a pin!

quickCheck.question: In the command digitalWrite(13, HIGH);, what does the number 13 mean?
options: Which pin number to turn on
quickCheck.explanation: The number 13 tells the Arduino exactly which pin header to send electricity to!
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Commands tell the board which pin to use. The number specifies the exact pin connection.

quickCheck.question: What does the word HIGH mean in digitalWrite(13, HIGH);?
quickCheck.explanation: In digital code, HIGH means turn the power ON so current flows to your component!
quickCheck.warmupExplanation: Think of HIGH like flipping a switch ON. LOW means flipping the switch OFF.

steps.title: How Text Turns Into Voltage
steps.markdownContent:
### The Code-to-Electricity Pipeline ⚡

How does English-like code in your editor turn into 5 Volts of physical electricity?

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Your Sketch (C++ Code)       │
│    digitalWrite(13, HIGH);      │
└────────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ Compiled into Machine Code
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 2. Flash Memory (Binary Bits)   │
│    10110001 00001101 00000001   │
└────────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ CPU Fetches & Executes Instruction
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 3. ATmega328P Internal Gate     │
│    Flips tiny silicon transistor│
└────────────────┬────────────────┘
                 │ Connects Pin 13 to +5V Rail
                 ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│ 4. Physical Header Pin 13       │
│    +5 Volts rushes out to LED!  │
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### Syntax Rules Matter!
- **Function Name**: `digitalWrite` (notice the capital 'W'—C++ is case sensitive!).
- **Parameters**: `(13, HIGH)` tells the function **WHERE** (Pin 13) and **WHAT** (HIGH / 5V).
- **The Semicolon**: `;` marks the end of a command. Forgetting it causes a compilation syntax error!

steps.title: Code Deconstruction Lab
steps.markdownContent:
### Deconstruct the Hardware Command! 🧩

Tap each token in the code statement below to break down its role in controlling physical hardware:
- `digitalWrite`: Built-in function verb.
- `(` and `)`: Parameter wrappers.
- `13`: Target digital pin on the Uno header.
- `,`: Parameter separator.
- `HIGH`: Output state setting pin to +5V.
- `;`: Statement terminator.

Interact with each piece to see its definition and watch the output state change!

steps.title: Code-to-Hardware Checkpoint
steps.markdownContent: Check your understanding of how code statements command electronic pins!

interactiveConfig.question: What happens if you forget the semicolon (;) at the end of a statement in C++?
options: The compiler will report a syntax error and refuse to upload
The Arduino will guess what you meant
The pin will catch on fire
interactiveConfig.explanation: In C++, semicolons are mandatory statement terminators. Omitting one stops compilation.

questions.question: What happens if you forget the semicolon (;) at the end of a statement in C++?
options: The compiler will report a syntax error and refuse to upload
The Arduino will guess what you meant
The pin will catch on fire
questions.explanation: In C++, semicolons are mandatory statement terminators. Omitting one stops compilation.

questions.question: Why is digitalWrite written with a capital 'W' instead of all lowercase?
options: C++ is case-sensitive and uses camelCase naming for functions
Capital letters run faster on the processor
To make the code take up more space
questions.explanation: C++ is strictly case-sensitive. Writing digitalwrite (all lowercase) will result in an unrecognized identifier error.

questions.question: To turn OFF an LED connected to Pin 13, which command should you write?
questions.explanation: In Arduino core syntax, LOW sets a pin to 0 Volts, turning off the connected LED.
